lesson.title: An Age of Reform: Meeting Industrial America's Problems with Government Power
lesson.summary: The Progressive Era, roughly the 1890s through the late 1910s, was a broad, loosely organized reform movement that used government at every level to address the social and economic problems created by rapid industrialization and urbanization.
lesson.body:
By the 1890s, the United States had transformed itself. Factories, railroads, and corporations had grown to a scale no one had planned for, cities had filled with immigrants and rural migrants faster than housing or sanitation could keep pace, and a small number of business owners controlled enormous shares of entire industries. The political system of the Gilded Age, with its patronage-driven parties and its comfortable relationships between officeholders and big donors, had shown little appetite or capacity to manage any of this. Progressivism grew out of the conviction, shared by an unusually wide range of Americans, that these problems were not inevitable and that organized, informed government action could fix them.

Progressives were never a single party or a unified movement with one leader or one platform. They included settlement house workers documenting slum conditions, city engineers pushing for clean water systems, ministers preaching a Social Gospel of Christian duty toward the poor, women's club members lobbying for child labor laws, and business owners who wanted predictable regulation rather than chaotic competition. What tied them together was a shared faith in expertise and a rejection of two ideas that had dominated the previous generation. The first was Social Darwinism, the belief that economic winners and losers reflected natural, almost biological fitness and that government should not interfere with that sorting. The second was the comfortable assumption, common in Gilded Age politics, that the job of government was mainly to protect property and stay out of the way. Progressives argued instead that unregulated markets produced avoidable suffering, that democracy itself had been captured by concentrated wealth, and that trained experts, whether sanitary engineers, economists, or social workers, could diagnose social ills the way doctors diagnosed disease.

Progressivism also absorbed and moderated ideas the Populist movement of the 1890s had raised more radically. Where the Populists had spoken for struggling farmers and pushed proposals like a graduated income tax and direct election of senators from outside the political mainstream, Progressives, who were disproportionately urban, middle class, and native born, took up many of the same causes and made them acceptable to a broader, more comfortable audience. Direct democracy tools such as the initiative, referendum, and recall spread through state constitutions. Cities experimented with commission and city manager governments meant to replace machine bosses with trained administrators. States passed workplace safety laws, limits on child labor, and pensions for widowed mothers.

At the national level, the era's energy found expression in three presidencies. Theodore Roosevelt, who became president in 1901, and later William Howard Taft and Woodrow Wilson all claimed the progressive label in different ways, and the era produced four constitutional amendments between 1913 and 1920: income tax, direct election of senators, prohibition, and women's suffrage. None of this reform impulse was free of contradiction. Many progressives supported immigration restriction, and Progressive Era reforms coexisted with, and sometimes reinforced, the era's deep racial segregation. Still, the basic premise of the Progressive Era, that an active, regulatory government answerable to an informed public could correct the excesses of industrial capitalism, reshaped the relationship between Americans and their government for the rest of the twentieth century.
